title: The Sound of Suchness
summary: When emptiness meets emptiness all dharmas rise; the singer remains, having fully realized the four moments, in cessation in the middle, where drop and nāda do not enter and whatever is sought as other is lost, and Kaṅkaṇa ends with a clamour of sound and everything shattered by the sound of suchness. Munidatta reads the meeting of emptinesses as the fourth state joining the third, self-blessing, through the vajra guru's blessing, so that the fruit, coupled union, arises (cp.44.m2); he places the middle in the madhyamā, the central channel (cp.44.m3), takes drop and nāda as the concepts of grasper and grasped (cp.44.m4), and makes the clamour the noise of novice yogins arguing over 'with form' and 'formless', broken by the sound of suchness (cp.44.m6).

flags.note: The poet's name is not in the Bengali heading. It is supplied from the attribution kauṅkaṇapādānāṃ, 'of Kauṅkaṇapāda', which Shastri prints before line 1a and which is not part of the verse; the Tibetan heading also names him (kaM ka Na'i zhabs). Drop '· Kaṅkaṇapāda' if headings should render only the heading line.

lines.gloss: in/with emptiness (sune) · emptiness (suna) · having met (miliā) · when (jabem̐)

flags.note: sune is locative or instrumental ('in' or 'with emptiness'), suna the subject; rendered 'has met with'. miliā could also be 'mingled' or 'merged'; 'met' keeps the plain sense of mil- and Munidatta's mīlati. The Tibetan mthun gyur, 'came into accord', agrees in sense.

lines.gloss: all-dharmas (saala 'all' + dhāma 'dharma') · risen (ūiā) · then (tabem̐) · (dhru: refrain cue, not translated)

flags.note: dhāma is taken as dharma, 'all dharmas', with Munidatta's lemma sarvadharma and the Tibetan chos rnams thams cad. Alternative: Sanskrit dhāman, 'abode, realm, light' ('then all realms have risen'). Kept as the keep-source term dharma, in the plural.

lines.gloss: am, remain (ācchu) · I (hum̐) · four moments (caukhaṇa) · having fully realized (saṃbohī)
lines.en: I remain, having fully realized the [four moments]{catuhksana}:

flags.note: hum̐ is read as the pronoun 'I' (not the syllable hūṃ) and saṃbohī as an absolutive, 'having fully realized', following Munidatta's paraphrase (saṃbodhayitvā tiṣṭhāmi, 'having awakened … I abide'). Alternatives: saṃbohī as the noun sambodhi, 'perfect awakening' ('I am, in the four moments, perfect awakening'); ācchu as 'being', as in the Tibetan (yod pa'i skad cig bzhi, 'the four moments of being'), which has no 'I'. 'Remain' for ācchu could also be 'am' or 'abide'.

lines.gloss: middle (mājha) · cessation (niroha) · unsurpassed (aṇuara) · awakening (bohī) · (dhru: refrain cue, not translated)

flags.note: The line is nominal; rendered as a juxtaposition, 'cessation in the middle, unsurpassed awakening'. The Tibetan has an instrumental, 'by cessation in the middle, unsurpassed awakening' (dbus su 'gog pas); one could also read 'the middle is cessation, awakening unsurpassed'. 'Middle' is the image; Munidatta's central channel stays in the notes.

Shastri divides ṇahim̐ e, 'not … here' (e, 'this, here'). Divided ṇa him̐e, the same letters give 'not … in the heart' (him̐e, locative of hia, 'heart'), which the Tibetan line supports: snying la 'jug pa med, 'do not enter the heart'. I kept Shastri's division; the alternative line is 'Drop and nāda have not entered the heart;'.
bindu is rendered with the glossary's 'drop'. Paired with nāda it is the dot of a seed syllable rather than a drop of vital essence, so the source form 'bindu' might serve better in this line.

lines.gloss: other (aṇa) · seeking, looking for (cāhante) · other (āṇa) · destroyed, lost (biṇaṭhā) · (dhru: refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: in seeking another, the other is lost.

flags.note: Chosen: 'in seeking another, the other is lost', keeping the repetition 'other … other'. Alternatives: 'looking elsewhere, the other is ruined' (the Tibetan gzhan du bltas pas, 'by looking elsewhere'); or 'looking for one, the other is lost', an either-or. biṇaṭhā (vinaṣṭa) is stronger than 'lost': 'destroyed, perished'.

lines.gloss: where / as (jathām̐) · you came (āilem̐si) · there / so (tathā) · know! (jāna)
lines.en: Where you came from, know it there;

flags.note: jathām̐ … tathā taken as 'where … there', as in Munidatta's 'from which … in that'; the Tibetan reads manner, 'as … so' ('as you came, so know'). jāna has no expressed object; 'it' is supplied.

lines.gloss: middle? (printed māsaṃ; Tibetan dbu ma) · staying (thākī) · all (saala) · abandoned? or dawn? (bihāṇa) · (dhru: refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: staying in the middle, all is left behind.

flags.note: Printed māsaṃ ('month', or māṃsa 'flesh') does not construe. 'Middle' follows the Tibetan line, dbu ma ru ni, 'in the middle', perhaps for mājhaṃ as in 2b. If the printed text is kept: 'staying a month, …' or 'staying in the flesh, …'.

bihāṇa taken as 'abandoned, left behind' (Sanskrit vihāna or vihīna; the Tibetan has rnam par spong, 'abandon'). Alternative: 'dawn, morning' (Prakrit vihāṇa, modern Bengali bihān), giving 'all is dawn', which would echo the rising of 1b.

lines.gloss: says (bhaṇai) · Kaṅkaṇa · clamour, clamorous (kalaela) · with sound (sādem̐)

flags.note: kalaela sādem̐, 'with a clamorous sound', may describe the voice in which Kaṅkaṇa speaks, or be an instrumental of agent parallel to tadhatānādem̐ in 5b ('with a clamorous sound … all was shattered'). Munidatta instead makes the clamour, of novice yogins, the thing that is broken. The comma after 'sound' leaves the first two open; Munidatta's reading is in the notes, not the line.
The Tibetan line reads kaM ka na smras ka la ya yi drin, 'Kaṅkaṇa said: by the grace of Ka-la-ya', transcribing kalaela as if it were a name and taking sādem̐ as 'grace'.

lines.gloss: all (sarbba) · was shattered, scattered (biccharila) · by the sound of suchness (tadhatā + nāda, instrumental) · (dhru: refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: all has been shattered by the sound of [suchness]{tathata}.

flags.note: biccharila rendered 'shattered', with Munidatta's bhagna, 'broken', and the Tibetan rnam bshig, 'demolished'. Alternative: 'overspread, filled' (Sanskrit vicchurita): 'all was filled with the sound of suchness'.

The Tibetan line adds 'unstruck' (gzhom med): 'the unstruck melody of suchness'. The Bengali has only tadhatānāda, 'the sound of suchness'; Munidatta's paraphrase has samatathatānāda, 'the sound of sameness and suchness'. Not translated.

notes.text: rāga: a melodic mode of Indian music. Each song is headed by the rāga it is sung to, here Mallārī, also the melody of song 30. Later Indian music knows a rainy-season rāga Mallār (Malhār); whether it is the same melody is uncertain.

The Bengali heading gives only the rāga. Shastri prints the attribution kauṅkaṇapādānāṃ, 'of Kauṅkaṇapāda', before the first line; it is not part of the verse and is rendered here in the heading, as the Tibetan heading also names the poet: mal+la rI zhes bya ba'i glu dbyangs kaM ka Na'i zhabs kyi'o, 'the melody called Mallārī, of Kaṅkaṇapāda'. The attribution spells the name with kau-, which might also be a derivative of the region-name Koṅkaṇa; this is uncertain. The poet calls himself Kaṅkaṇa, Sanskrit for 'bracelet' (5a), and Munidatta calls him the siddha master Kaṅkaṇa and Kaṅkaṇapāda (cp.44.m1, cp.44.m6). In the Tibetan translation of Munidatta's opening sentence he is keng rus zhabs, with keng rus, 'skeleton', as if the name were read kaṅkāla.

Munidatta introduces the song: the siddha master Kaṅkaṇa, delighted by drinking the liquor (āsava) of supreme compassion, explains that same meaning in other words (cp.44.m1). The Tibetan translation has 'nectar' (bdud rtsi) for the liquor and 'the meaning of reality' (de kho na nyid kyi don) for 'that same meaning', as it does again where Munidatta introduces the refrain (cp.44.m3).

sune suna: the same word twice, first in the locative or instrumental (sune, 'in' or 'with emptiness'), then as subject (suna). miliā is a participle of mil-, 'meet, join, mingle'. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has stong par stong nyid gang tshe mthun gyur pa, 'when emptiness has come into accord with the empty'.

Munidatta reads the first emptiness (sune) as 'the third', the emptiness of self-blessing (svādhiṣṭhāna), and the second (suna) as 'the fourth state', emptiness, which meets it of itself through the blessing of the vajra guru; 'then', at that moment, 'all dharmas' means that the fruit, coupled union (yuganaddha), arises (cp.44.m2). The song itself names no guru and counts no emptinesses. The Tibetan comment speaks of 'the emptiness of blessing' without 'third'.

saaladhāma: saala is 'all' (Sanskrit sakala). dhāma is taken as dharma, 'phenomenon', by Munidatta, whose lemma is sarvadharma, 'all dharmas' (cp.44.m2), and by the Tibetan translation (chos rnams thams cad, 'all dharmas'); the same spelling stands for dharma elsewhere in these songs. Sanskrit dhāman, 'abode, domain, light', is the other possibility ('all realms', 'all lights'). ūiā, 'risen' (Sanskrit udita), is the word for a sun or moon coming up; the Tibetan has 'char ba, 'dawn, appear'.

ācchu is from āch-, 'be, remain' (modern Bengali āche); hum̐ is the first-person pronoun 'I' (Apabhraṃśa hauṃ), not the seed syllable hūṃ. saṃbohī is read as an absolutive, 'having fully realized' (Sanskrit saṃbodhya), not as the noun sambodhi: Munidatta paraphrases 'having awakened the fourth joy through the moment beginning with vicitra, I abide (tiṣṭhāmi)' (cp.44.m3). The Tibetan line, yod pa'i skad cig bzhi la yang dag rtogs, 'fully realizes in the four moments of being', takes ācchu as 'being' (yod pa), has no 'I', and renders saṃbohī with a verb, yang dag rtogs, 'fully realize'.

The four moments (caukhaṇa) are, in the Hevajra system, the four phases of yogic union, vicitra ('variety'), vipāka, vimarda and vilakṣaṇa, matched with the four joys. Munidatta, introducing the refrain as saying the same meaning again, has the singer abide having awakened the fourth joy through the moment beginning with vicitra, and quotes the Hevajra (the Dvikalpa): 'There the joys arise…' (cp.44.m3).

mājha is 'middle', the place between; the line does not say middle of what. Munidatta's paraphrase, 'thereby I am cessation in the madhyamā' (madhyamānirodha), puts the madhyamā, the central channel of the subtle body, where the song has the middle; the Tibetan comment has dbu mar 'gog pa, 'cessation in the central one', and adds 'by self-blessing' (rang byin gyis brlabs pas) where the Sanskrit has 'thereby I'. He then says unsurpassed awakening is gained from the faults of the seven natures and the stains of samādhi (cp.44.m3); the word that links them, Sanskrit nidhānāt, 'from the store', Tibetan gzhi las, 'from the ground', is hard to construe and may be corrupt.

biduṇāda is bidu (bindu) and ṇāda (nāda) as a pair. nāda, 'sound, resonance': in mantra meditation the subtle sound into which a seed syllable dissolves, drawn as a fine stroke above the bindu, the dot of the nasal. Here bindu is rendered with the glossary's 'drop'. The Tibetan translation keeps both words (thig le nA da). Song 32 also says there is no nāda and no bindu.

The Tibetan line, thig le nA da snying la 'jug pa med, 'drop and nāda do not enter the heart', has 'heart' (snying) where the Bengali as printed has ṇahim̐ e, 'not … here' or 'this'. Shastri's word division is editorial: divided ṇa him̐e, the same letters give 'not … in the heart', with him̐e as the locative of hia, 'heart'; the form hiem̐ is attested in song 28. The translation keeps Shastri's division and flags the alternative.

Munidatta introduces couplet 3, his second verse, as stating practice (the Tibetan: 'the fruit of practice'). His lemma is 'nāda and so on', as though his text began with nāda; he mentions the long syllable hūṃ, then explains bindu as the conceptual thought of the knowledge that grasps means (upāya), and nāda as the conceptual thought of the knowledge of the grasped, wisdom (prajñā): at that time both are given up as conceptual thought (cp.44.m4). Shastri's nāpāya- is unclear; the Tibetan thabs 'dzin pa, 'grasping means', supports upāya.

aṇa … āṇa are both 'other' (Sanskrit anya); cāhante is a present participle of cāh-, 'look, seek, want'; biṇaṭhā is 'destroyed, lost' (Sanskrit vinaṣṭa). The Tibetan translation has gzhan du bltas pas gzhan ni rnam par nyams, 'by looking elsewhere, the other is ruined'. Munidatta does not paraphrase the line word by word; he goes on: seeing the non-apprehension of all dharmas, even the awakening of mind (cittabodhana) has perished for me (cp.44.m4). The Tibetan comment has instead that realizing the mind, too, is not apprehended.

jathām̐ … tathā is a correlative pair, 'where … there' or 'as … so'; āilem̐si is a past second-person form, 'you came'; jāna is an imperative, 'know', with no object expressed. Munidatta reads the pair as 'from which … in that' and supplies the object: from which bodhicitta ('mind of awakening') you were born in the beginning, in that, your own bodhicitta, free of the conceptual thought of senses and objects, know what has the form of the experience of the fourth bliss (cp.44.m5). The Tibetan line reads manner: ji ltar 'ongs pa de ltar shes par gyur, 'as one came, so one comes to know'.

Munidatta introduces couplet 4, his third verse, as stating the phāratā of conventional bodhicitta (cp.44.m5); the word is unclear (perhaps sphāratā, 'spreading'), and the Tibetan has byed pa nyid, 'activity'. In his paraphrase Shastri prints indu, 'moon', where the Tibetan has dbang po, 'senses', so indriya is probably meant. He supports the reading with a dohā of Saraha that is corrupt in the edition; in the Tibetan it speaks of the mind become steady and of the same taste as the wind.

Shastri prints māsaṃ, which as it stands gives 'month' (māsa) or 'flesh' (māṃsa), neither of which construes. The Tibetan line, dbu ma ru ni thams cad rnam par spong, 'in the middle, all is abandoned', suggests its manuscript had a word for 'middle' here, perhaps mājhaṃ, as in the refrain (2b); the translation follows it. bihāṇa is taken with the Tibetan (rnam par spong, 'abandon') as from Sanskrit vihāna or vihīna, 'abandonment, abandoned'; Prakrit vihāṇa, 'dawn, morning' (modern Bengali bihān), would give 'all is dawn'. Munidatta does not quote this line; his 'free of (virahita) the conceptual thought of senses and objects' (cp.44.m5) may stand where the song has saala bihāṇa, which would favour 'abandoned'.

The poet names himself here (the bhaṇitā): Kaṅkaṇa, Sanskrit for 'bracelet'. kalaela is kalakala, a confused noise, a din or clamour; sādem̐ is the instrumental of sāda (Sanskrit śabda), 'with a sound'. In the line the clamour qualifies a sound: either the voice in which Kaṅkaṇa speaks or, read with the parallel instrumental tadhatānādem̐ in 5b, the noise with which all is shattered. The comma in the translation leaves both open.

The Tibetan line reads kaM ka na smras ka la ya yi drin, 'Kaṅkaṇa said: by the grace (drin) of Ka-la-ya', transcribing kalaela as if it were a name and taking sādem̐ as 'grace' (Sanskrit prasāda). Its translation of Munidatta's comment, however, has ca co, 'noise', for kalakala (cp.44.m6).

Munidatta introduces the last couplet as setting out the poet's own power, and paraphrases: the siddha master Kaṅkaṇapāda says that the clamour of novice yogins about 'with form', 'formless' and the like (sākāra, nirākāra) is broken by the sound of sameness and suchness (samatathatānāda) (cp.44.m6). He thus makes the clamour the thing that is shattered, the 'all' of 5b, where the song has the clamour as a quality of the sound in Kaṅkaṇa's own line; the two are not harmonized in the translation. He adds a verse of scripture: 'By the lion's roar of emptiness all enemies are terrified.' The Tibetan comment has ca co, 'noise', for the clamour, 'the unstruck sound of sameness' (mnyam pa nyid gzhom du med pa'i sgra) for the sound of sameness and suchness, and 'all sounds' (sgra rnams thams cad) for 'all enemies'.

biccharila is a past form, 'was scattered, shattered'. Munidatta's paraphrase has bhagna, 'broken' (cp.44.m6), and the Tibetan line rnam bshig, 'demolished'; Sanskrit vicchurita, 'overspread, inlaid', would instead give 'all was filled with the sound of suchness'. tadhatānādem̐ is tadhatā (tathatā, 'suchness') with nāda, 'sound', in the instrumental, 'by the sound of suchness'; nāda is rendered 'sound' here, not kept in source form as in 3a. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293), thams cad rnam bshig de nyid gzhom med dbyangs, has 'the unstruck melody of suchness': 'unstruck' (gzhom med, Sanskrit anāhata) is not in the Bengali, and Munidatta has sama-, 'sameness', in its place.

termsOmitted.reason: Tibetan hit only (dbu ma). The Bengali word (printed māsaṃ, read with the Tibetan as 'middle') is rendered 'middle', the image, as mājha is in 2b; 'central channel' is Munidatta's reading and stays in the notes.
Tibetan hit only (drin, 'grace'): the Tibetan reads sādem̐ as 'grace', while the Bengali is rendered 'sound'. See the witness note on 5a.
Tibetan hit only (gzhom med, 'unstruck'): the word is not in the Bengali, so it is not translated. See the witness note on 5b.
Not a detected hit; listed for clarity. The nāda in tadhatānādem̐ is rendered 'sound' ('the sound of suchness'), the general sense, not the keep-source term nāda of 3a.

proposals.definition: The middle, the space between (Old Bengali mājha, from Sanskrit madhya). The refrain of song 44 sets cessation in the middle (2b) without saying middle of what. Munidatta's paraphrase has 'cessation in the madhyamā', the central channel, in its place (cp.44.m3); the Tibetan line has dbus, 'centre'.

symbolicReadings.referent: the madhyamā, the central channel: his paraphrase of the refrain has 'cessation in the madhyamā' (madhyamānirodha) where the song has mājha niroha, with no explicit gloss; the Tibetan comment agrees (dbu mar 'gog pa)

proposals.rationale: The plain word for 'middle' is the kind of image the commentary reads as the central channel, and it is likely to recur (mājha, mājhe). An entry lets it be marked as an image and keeps 'central channel' (the madhyama entry, which renders Munidatta's madhyamā) out of the verse line.

forms.translit: rnam pa dang bcas pa dang rnam pa med pa
forms.lemma: rnam pa dang bcas pa, rnam pa med pa

proposals.definition: 'With form' (sākāra) and 'formless' (nirākāra): opposed Buddhist positions on whether awareness really bears the images of its objects, argued among later Yogācāra thinkers. Munidatta names them, 'and the like', as the clamour of novice yogins that the sound of sameness and suchness breaks (cp.44.m6). The Tibetan has rnam pa dang bcas pa and rnam pa med pa.
proposals.rationale: A doctrinal pair in Munidatta's comment on the last couplet, already named in the kalakala entry's reading; the weave of cp.44.m6 needs a fixed rendering, and the pair may recur in his comments.

questions: 4b is the line I am least sure of. Do you accept 'middle' for the printed māsaṃ on the Tibetan's evidence (dbu ma ru), and 'all is left behind' for saala bihāṇa (Tibetan rnam par spong) rather than 'all is dawn'? Or should the line keep the printed text ('staying a month' / 'in the flesh') with the Tibetan reading in a note?
3a: keep Shastri's division ṇahim̐ e ('have not entered here'), or read ṇa him̐e ('have not entered the heart'), as the Tibetan (snying la) suggests?

5a: I wrote the poet's self-naming as 'Kaṅkaṇa', the source form (keep-source), rather than the entry's 'Kaṅkaṇapāda', since the poet would not add the honorific -pāda to his own name. Should p-kankana list 'Kaṅkaṇa' as a variant?
Heading: I added '· Kaṅkaṇapāda' from the attribution kauṅkaṇapādānāṃ (emended out of 1a), following the pattern 'Rāga … · poet'; the Bengali heading itself names only the rāga. Keep or drop?

2a: please confirm hum̐ as 'I' and saṃbohī as the absolutive 'having fully realized', and 'remain' for ācchu (or 'abide', after Munidatta's tiṣṭhāmi). The bodhi entry lists saṃbohem̐ from another song as a form of bodhi; if forms like saṃbohī are verbal, that entry may need narrowing so they are not taken for 'awakening'.

5a–5b: is 'Kaṅkaṇa says, with a clamour of sound, / all has been shattered by the sound of suchness' acceptable as a way of leaving open whether the clamour is his voice or the noise of the shattering, with Munidatta's reading (the novice yogins' clamour is what is broken) kept in the notes? And 'shattered' rather than 'overspread' for biccharila?
3a: in the pair bindu and nāda (the dot and the stroke of a seed syllable), is the glossary's 'drop' right, or should bindu stay 'bindu' here?
1b: 'all dharmas' (keep-source dharma in the plural) for saaladhāma, as both witnesses read it, or 'all realms' / 'all lights' (dhāman)?
4a: I supplied 'it' as the object of jāna ('know it there'). Would you prefer the Tibetan's reading of manner, 'as you came, so know'?
